title: Watching This Video Disqualifies You From Jury Duty for Life
beats: You on a jury know two options; a secret third one that watching this may disqualify you for.
Defines jury nullification: guilty beyond doubt but jurors acquit anyway; warning it can get you arrested.
Not a lawyer, not legal advice disclaimer.
Nullification is not a law but the logical consequence of two rules: no punishing juries, no double jeopardy.
Restates: words don't match thoughts, protected by both rules.
Lawyers argue about it like physicists about quantum mechanics: hard to observe, philosophically loaded.
Fugitive slave acquittals vs lynch-mob acquittals: same mechanism, opposite moral valence.
Guilty-direction nullification exists too; only rule 1 protects it, so it is weaker.
Voir dire question: answer yes and be rejected, answer no and commit perjury; optimal strategy is silence.
Silence makes coordinating with 11 other jurors risky, limiting nullification as reform tool; plea bargain aside.
Courts universally refuse to tell jurors; mock-trial evidence that telling them shifts verdicts by sympathy.
Returns to three framings (righteous will, anarchy, citizen lawmaking); system leaves it to you; it will always exist.

theory: Grey turns a contested topic into a derivation: two uncontroversial rules plus logic force nullification to exist, so the viewer cannot dismiss it as a loophole. He then runs the same two rules forward into strategy and policy, and uses paired moral examples to keep the evaluative question open rather than answering it.
velocity: Orchestrator playbook 'emergent phenomenon': state 2-3 simple rules on screen, then ask the learner what must follow before revealing it.
Scene builder: keep the rule list pinned as a persistent panel and highlight which rule applies at each step (as at 2:00-2:18).
For value-laden topics, always pair a sympathetic and an unsympathetic example of the same mechanism.
Second-person role: put the learner in the decision seat (juror at voir dire) to surface dilemmas.
Evals: give a new variant (guilty-direction) and check the learner can say which rules still apply.
